title: Claude Opus 5.5 finished Baldur's Gate 3 on its own in 39 hours
content:
Claude Opus 5.5 finished Baldur's Gate 3 on its own in 39 hours
A half-orc paladin named Claude, 96 sessions, $712 of API usage, a mod, a tool server and nobody at the controls. What the agent saw each turn, where it got stuck, and the one result I had to rerun.
On 18 October at 11:35, a half-orc paladin named Claude killed the Netherbrain on the twelfth attempt and Baldur's Gate 3 played its ending. The player was Claude Opus 5.5, working through a mod and a tool server I built for it, with nobody at the controls. It took 96 sessions and 38.9 hours of play. Along the way it broke its paladin's oath twice for good, paid 3,000 gold to get it back, and acted on a promise it had made 34 sessions earlier.
I had just started playing Baldur's Gate 3 myself when it struck me that the game would be a good test for an AI, both of how well it thinks and of how well it can play a character. It is a long role-playing game: your character carries a mind-flayer tadpole in their head, travels with companions who have their own stories, and ends by fighting the Netherbrain, the giant brain that controls the tadpoles. Fights are turn-based tactics decided by dice, conversations end in skill checks, and many choices are permanent.
One run, with a harness I kept fixing along the way, shows that the game can be finished like this. It doesn't say how good the agent is. The caveats are at the end.
The setup
The game was the native Linux build of Baldur's Gate 3 (Patch 8 Hotfix 10) on Explorer difficulty. The agent was Claude Opus 5.5 at medium reasoning effort (an API setting), running in Claude Code with every built-in tool switched off, so its only tools were the 93 that my server exposes.
One turn, as the agent sees it
Viconia is a late boss whose cultists keep filling the room with magical Darkness, which blinds anyone inside it. The agent lost to her twelve times. On the thirteenth attempt, in session 82, it found that Daylight cast at a point on the ground works while blinded, though Daylight cast at an ally fails. This is that turn. The agent sends Shadowheart's whole turn as one call: cast Daylight at a point and skip any reaction prompt.
combat_turn(who="Shadowheart", wait_turn=60, plan={"action":[{"ability":"Daylight","x,y,z":"-377,29,-1645"}],"on_reaction":"skip"})
the agent's call
TURN e3 Shadowheart (round 1) — waited 11.8s for the turn — reaction prompt: declined (done) action: Target_Daylight_Container: took the first variant Target_Daylight → Target_Daylight: done — statuses=[e333 Daylight] NOW e3 hp=154/160 action=0 bonus=1 movement=12 reaction=1 CHANGES e331 Cambion HP 160->148/164, +Bone Chilled -Blinded e2 Gale -Blinded e3 Shadowheart -Blinded -Covert Critical e4 Claude -Blinded + e317 Sharran Novice Dohna hostile dead 15m + e284 Sharran Fidelian Gydd hostile HP 51/51 16m NEXT e295 Sharran Fidelian Hyrald, e288 Sharran Sentry Baxta, … then e331 Cambion (yours): send its combat_turn now
what the server sent back (lightly trimmed)
The reply says what changed: Blinded dropped off Gale, Shadowheart and Claude, and off the Cambion, a devil the party had summoned. One of the Darkness casters, Sharran Fidelian Gydd, is now in view 16 metres away. Short handles like e284 stand in for the game's internal IDs. The agent's next call played the Cambion's turn: Rays of Fire at two of the cultists. Once the party could see, Gale's upcast Magic Missile, which never misses, killed Viconia in round 1.
The pieces
A Lua mod runs inside the game, loaded through bg3le, a community Linux port of the Script Extender. A Python MCP server turns the game state into short text and tool calls into game actions. The agent sees only what a party member can perceive, by the engine's own line-of-sight checks, and only what the game's UI shows. It can take a screenshot whenever it wants, and it can read bg3.wiki, the way a player with the wiki on a second screen would; it did 577 times. Its instructions contain no puzzle or encounter answers. One tool leaked one, in the Faith-Leap Trial, and I come back to that below.
Its memory is a folder of Markdown files in git that it writes itself. Each session starts with a fresh context and the last session's handoff note, and runs on a 20 to 45 minute clock. The run came in two stretches: sessions 1 to 65 from 9 to 11 October, then a six-day pause while I rebuilt parts of the harness, then sessions 66 to 96 on 17 and 18 October.
The whole run, in numbers:
Fig 2
The ten tools it reached for most
Calls across all 96 sessions. Source: [tool] lines in S*.log.
combat_turn plays a character's whole turn (move, action, bonus action, end) in one call. wait_for lets the agent keep planning while a walk or a spell plays out instead of blocking on it. The 863 screenshots and 583 raw clicks were the fallback for whatever the text tools couldn't handle yet.
What a fight looks like
I didn't record video during the run, so on 15 October I replayed one fight from the save before it: Malus Thorm, the surgeon who runs the House of Healing. Claude Sonnet 5.5, the cheaper model, played the replay, since it's only an illustration. It gets Malus from 193 HP down to 7 before the party falls, then writes itself a lesson and reloads.
Fig 4
Story progress over 38.9 hours of play
Cumulative progress points after each session (quests, named kills, new areas, key items), as the harness scores them. Shaded: the four longest stalls. Each dot is a boss at the moment it was beaten; hover or tap one for the fight. Sources: progress_history.jsonl, the fight records and the session logs.
The score is the harness's own: points for quests, named kills, new areas and key items. Flat stretches are where the run stalled: the Gauntlet of Shar and the Shadowfell (four and a half hours), Gortash and Orin (nearly four), Cazador and Viconia (three and a half) and, at the end, the Netherbrain. The dashed line is the six-day pause.
The paladin's oath
The agent named its character Claude and took the Oath of Devotion: be honest, protect the innocent, keep your word. In this game the oath has teeth. Break it and the paladin becomes an Oathbreaker; to get the Devotion oath back you pay the Oathbreaker Knight, who turns up at camp, and the price rises every time.
Its instructions allowed a reload only after a party wipe or a clear accident such as a misclick, never to reroll a failed dialogue check. It broke the oath twice for good. In the House of Healing, Confusion made Claude read a Scroll of Cloudkill, and the cloud killed an innocent patient. The agent counted that as a game outcome and paid the Oathbreaker Knight 1,000 gold, leaving 43. Two sessions later Claude's crossbow killed a prison warden who had turned hostile only because the party was caught. That cost 2,000; the agent saved for eleven sessions and paid, with 60 gold left over.
[decision] Claude's OATH IS BROKEN (Confused Claude cast Silence and read the Scroll of Cloudkill; the cloud killed the Distressed Patient). No reload: a game outcome, not a misclick.
session log · S026 · 09:33
A third break it reloaded away. At the Steel Watch Foundry, Claude ordered a gnome engineer to set off the factory's self-destruct, and the oath broke again. The agent reloaded, which stretched its own rule, noted from the wiki that a third restoration would cost 10,000 gold, and had Wyll, who isn't a paladin, give the order instead. Human players do the same.
Other mistakes stayed. The agent misread an option at Lae'zel's cage and sided with the tieflings shooting at her, so the githyanki warrior never joined; it didn't reload, because that "would only reroll the checks". Jaheira ran ahead in Moonrise Towers and died for good. A misclick fed Claude's Gloves of Power to Gale, a wizard whose curse makes him eat magic items.
It also policed itself. In the Gauntlet of Shar, an Act 2 temple of trials, Gale's Spell Slot Restoration seemed to cost nothing, so the agent stopped using it and reported a possible bug:
[note] fairness/bug for operator: Gal

report.summary: An AI agent powered by Claude Opus 5.5 autonomously completed Baldur’s Gate 3 in 96 sessions over 38.9 hours using a custom mod and tool server.
report.background: Large language model agents are increasingly tested on long, open-ended tasks rather than short prompts. Games are attractive sandboxes because they combine planning, tool use, memory, combat tactics, dialogue and irreversible consequences. Baldur’s Gate 3 is especially demanding: turn-based dice combat, party companions, permanent choices and a long campaign. The author built a harness around a Lua mod, a community Linux port of the Script Extender and a Python MCP server that converts game state into short text and tool calls into actions. The agent had no built-in tools, a fresh context each session and a git-backed Markdown memory folder.
key_points: The run used a native Linux copy of Baldur’s Gate 3 on Explorer difficulty, with Claude Opus 5.5 at medium reasoning effort in Claude Code. All built-in tools were disabled; the agent could only use 93 tools exposed by a custom Python MCP server. It played 96 sessions totaling 38.9 hours and spent $712 on API usage.

Because each session started with a fresh context window, the agent kept its memory in a git-tracked folder of Markdown files. It wrote handoff notes and ran on a 20–45 minute clock. The run paused for six days while the operator rebuilt parts of the harness, showing that long-horizon autonomy still depends on careful scaffolding.

The agent’s most-used tool, combat_turn, played a character’s entire turn—movement, action, bonus action and end—in one call. wait_for let it plan while animations played. It also took 863 screenshots, made 583 raw clicks and read bg3.wiki 577 times, using text tools first and falling back to UI-level actions.

The paladin’s oath created persistent consequences. Claude broke its Oath of Devotion twice, paying 3,000 gold total to restore it, and acted on a promise made 34 sessions earlier. It reloaded only after party wipes or clear accidents, though it made an exception at the Steel Watch Foundry. Mistakes such as losing Lae’zel and Jaheira stayed in the run.

The author stresses this is one run with a harness that was still being repaired, not a measure of general agent skill. One result had to be rerun, no video was recorded during the original playthrough, and a tool leaked an answer in the Faith-Leap Trial. The result demonstrates feasibility, not robust benchmark performance.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the run is a useful example of long-horizon agent evaluation: memory, tool design, error recovery and cost matter as much as model reasoning. For developers, it shows how an MCP-style server can wrap a complex application into compact text observations and atomic actions, and why harness engineering is central. For regular users, it hints at agents that can pursue multi-day goals in software, but also at brittle failure modes and high API costs. The single-run, operator-assisted setup means it should be read as a proof of concept, not a product milestone. Reproducibility and independent testing are still needed.
report.tools: Follow BG3 Script Extender and its Linux port bg3le, the Lua modding layer, and the Python MCP server pattern used here. Claude Code is the agent runtime; MCP is the tool protocol. bg3.wiki is the information source the agent used. For broader work, watch open-source agent harnesses that combine git-backed memory, screenshots and structured tool calls.
